title: New communities
hook: Iona, Taizé, Bose and others: new monastic communities of mixed traditions

segments.voice: Yesterday, ekklesia, an arena and a pot of soup, and your line was where two or three.

A small island off the west coast of Scotland. Beside an old abbey church stand the ruins of the buildings where monks once lived, roofless, grass growing inside the walls. Then a Scottish minister named George MacLeod arrives with a crew: young ministers in training and out-of-work stonemasons and carpenters, side by side. They live, eat and pray together morning and evening, and rebuild the ruins, stone by stone. Out of that work came the Iona Community.

These new communities borrowed the old monastic shape and opened the doors to Christians of more than one church. Iona's members are scattered in ordinary jobs and homes, and keep a shared rule of prayer, money and action for justice. In a village in France, a Swiss Protestant called Brother Roger began a community at Taizé, and brothers from Catholic and Protestant backgrounds joined him. Young people came from across Europe to stay a week, and Taizé gave them a way of praying anyone can join: short lines from scripture, sung over and over, until the words sing themselves. In Italy, at Bose, men and women from different churches gathered to live by prayer, work and hospitality. None of these asks anyone to give up their own church. They ask for something older: life in common. The book of Acts describes the first believers, in the King James Bible: "And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common." A psalm sings how that feels from the inside: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" These communities have their own struggles; living together is hard, and their members say so. But each took the ancient habits, set hours of prayer, shared meals, shared work, a guest always welcome, and handed them to people who never expected to become monks.

`TAIZÉ: SHORT LINES, SUNG OVER AND OVER.`

segments.voice: Pray the Taizé way with the psalm, behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity: say it slowly, then again, then again softer, letting the breath set the pace, or use another short line from scripture that suits you. Don't push for meaning; let the repetition carry you, as it does in a room at Taizé. If you don't pray, repeat the words as a wish for the people you live and work with.
New communities. Iona, Taizé, Bose and others: communities that took the old monastic habits of prayer, work and shared life and opened them to Christians of different churches.
Your line: old ways, new people. The old rule had room for more than one church. Day nine hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Visitors to Taizé, Iona and similar communities join the community's daily rhythm of common prayer, meals and work, and Taizé-style prayer, with short chants sung over and over, is held in parishes of different churches.

notes: No dates given (Iona Community 1938, Taizé 1940, Bose 1965) per the claims rule.
'For a long time, a monastery usually meant one church's tradition' is a sweeping historical claim; soften or cut if a Keeper prefers. Anglican and Lutheran religious communities are not mentioned.

Iona: MacLeod (Church of Scotland) rebuilt the abbey's living quarters with trainee ministers and unemployed craftsmen; the abbey church itself had been partly restored earlier. 'put the roof back on' simplifies; confirm.
Iona Community members' rule (prayer, accounting for money and time, action for justice and peace): summarized; confirm.
Taizé: Brother Roger Schütz, Swiss Reformed; brothers now from Catholic and Protestant backgrounds. Confirm.

Bose: founded by Enzo Bianchi; men and women from different churches. The 2020 Vatican intervention that required Bianchi to leave is not mentioned ('These communities have their own struggles'). Confirm whether to address.
